texts.facts: 1. This is a complaint instituted under Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 (hereinafter referred to as 'PFA Act') for violation of section 2(ia)(a)(b)(m) and section 7 punishable under section 16 of PFA Act. 2. Brief facts leading to filing of the present complaint are that on 05.11.2010 at about 11.30 am, Food Inspector Sh. V.P.S. Chaudhary, purchased a sample of Coconut Laddoo, a food article, for analysis from Sh. Jagjit Singh, M/s. Jagjit Halwai, Shop No. 4, Behind Hanuman Mandir, Seva Nagar, New Delhi-110003, where the said food article was found stored for sale for human consumption and whereas Sh. Jagjit Singh was found vending of the said food article at the time of taking the sample. That the sample consisted of 1500 gm. of Coconut Laddoo taken from open tray bearing no declaration. That the same was taken under the supervision of Sh. P.R. Jha, SDM/LHA. That the sample was taken after proper mixing with the help of clean and dry spoon in clean and dry tray. That the said food articles was divided into three equal parts then and there by putting in three clean and dry glass bottles and 40 drops of formalin was added in each counter part of sample. That each bottle containing the sample was separately packed, fastened and sealed according to the PFA Act, 1954 and Rules 1955. That the vendor's signatures were obtained on the LHA slip and wrapper of the bottles containing the sample. That notice in Form VI was given to Sh. Jagjit Singh and the price of sample was also paid to him vide vendor receipt dated 05.11.2010. That Panchnama too was prepared at the spot and all the documents prepared by Food Inspector were signed by Sh. Jagjit Singh and by the other witness Sh. Shivji Mahto, F.A. That before starting the sample proceedings, efforts were made to get the public witnesses to join the proceedings but none came forward, as such Sh. Shivji Mahto, F.A. was joined as witness. That one part of the sample bearing LHA code No. 71/LHA/30123 along-with copy of memo VII and another copy of memo VII separately in intact condition were sent to Public Analyst and two remaining counterparts of the sample along-with two copies of memo VII were deposited with SDM/LHA in intact conditions. That all copies of memo VII were bearing the the seal impression of the seal by which the sample was sealed. That the Public Analyst analysed the sample and found the sample to be adulterated. The Public Analyst had given his report vide report No. PFA/Enf/3232/2010 dated 20.11.2010 wherein he opined, "The sample is adulterated because it contains added vegetable oil which is not declared as ingredient." 3. It is further averred that Sh. Jagjit Singh was the vendor cum proprietor of M/s. Jagjit Halwai, Shop No. 4, Behind Hanuman Mandir, Sewa Nagar, New Delhi-111003 at the time of taking sample and as such he is in-charge of and responsible for day to day conduct of the business of the said shop and responsible for complying with the provisions of the PFA Act 1954 and the Rules made thereunder. It is alleged that he has violated the provisions of Section 7 of the PFA Act, 1954 read with Section 2(ia) (a), (b) & (m) of PFA Act, 1954 which is punishable under section 16(1)(a) of the PFA Act, 1954. Da vs Jagjit Singh on 20 August, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/109557362/ 2 4. Upon filing of the present complaint, cognizance was taken vide order dated 23.03.2021. Upon service of summons, appearance was entered by accused and after complying with the provision under section 207 Cr.P.C, vide order dated 09.06.2011, notice for the offences under section 2(ia)(a)(b)&(m) punishable under section 16(1)(a) read with section 7 of PFA Act was served upon the accused to which he pleaded not guilty and claimed trial. Thereafter, the case was fixed for prosecution evidence. 5. The prosecution examined Sh V.P.S Chaudhary, Food Inspector as PW-1 who deposed that on 005.11.2010, he had visited the shop of the accused where accused Jagjit Singh was found conducting the business of sale of 'Coconut Laddoo'. That after disclosing his identity, he purchased 1500 grams of coconut Laddoo from an open aluminum tub having no label declaration, after properly mixing with the help of clean and dry spoon in a clean and dry tray. As per PW-1 he paid Rs.150/- vide vendors receipt Ex.PW1/A as sample price. That after lifting of sample, it was divided into three parts as per procedure prescribed under the PFA Act and Rules and separately packed and sealed in clean and dry glass bottles. That vendor signatures were obtained on the LHA slip. That thereafter, one counter part of the sample was deposited with the public analyst (PA) on 06.11.2010 and remaining two counterparts were deposited with the LHA. PW-1 further deposed that on receipt of the PA report Ex PW1/H the sample was found to be adulterarted, thereafter he sent a letter ExPW1/H to STO Ward No. 99 to disclose the constitution of M/s Jagjit Halwai shop. That as per reply received, no such firm of the accused was found registered with the Sales Tax. PW-1 further deposed that after obtaining due sanction of the Director, PFA the present complaint was filed against the accused person. PW-1 relied upon following documents: 1. Ex. PW 1/A : Vendor's Receipt; 2. Ex. PW 1/B : Notice in Form VI; 3. Ex. PW 1/C : Panchnama; 4. Ex. PW1/D : Raid Report under Rule 9(e); 5. Ex.PW1/E : Photocopy of Election ID of FBO; 5. Ex. PW 1/F : PA receipt; 6. Ex. PW 1/G : LHA receipt; 7. Ex. PW 1/H : PA Report; 8. Ex. PW 1/I : Letter to STO Ward No. 99; 9. Ex. PW1/J :Consent for prosecution; 10.Ex. PW1 / K : Present Complaint; Da vs Jagjit Singh on 20 August, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/109557362/ 3 11. ExPW1/L : Intimation letter along with PA report; 12. Ex.PW1/M : Copy of postal registration receipts; PW1 was duly cross-examined by Ld. Counsel for the accused. 6. Prosecution examined Sh. Shivji Mehto, FA, as PW-2 deposed on similar lines as PW-1 and identified his signatures on relevant documents. PW-2 however, could not be cross- examined as he expired. 7. The prosecution examined Sh.P.R. Jha as PW-3 who deposed on similar lines as PW-1. PW-3 was cross-examined by counsel for the accused. 8. No other witness was examined by the prosecution and thereafter, the prosecution evidence was closed. The statement of accused under section 313 Cr.P.C was recorded on 02.09.2022. The Ld. Predecessor of this Court, after hearing arguments, vide judgment dated 17.12.2022 convicted the accused. 9. In compliance of the directions of Ld. Sessions Court, the statement of the accused under section 313 Cr.P.C was recorded afresh on 09.01.2024. Thereafter, the accused led defence evidence. 10. The accused examined Sh. S.M Bhardwaj, Public Analyst as DW1 who deposed that he conducted analysis of the food sample 'Coconut Ladoo' from 09.11.2010 to 11.11.2010 and prepared the report on 20.11.2010 Ex.PW1/H. That as per his report, the sample was found adulterated as it was containing added vegetable oil which was not declared as an ingredient. That he has received the sample loose in a sealed sample bottle without the original label. He deposed in cases of loose sample, there are no original labels and thus it was not received. That in order to conduct test on the loose sample, he relied upon the ingredient disclosed in the Form No. VI, wherein the ingredients are stated by the FBO himself. That he received the Form No. VI along with sample for analysis. He clarified that he has received Form VII not Form VI. That Form VII was not available on judicial record, however, there was a description of Form VII in para No. 1 page 2 at point A in complaint. That he could not tell whether Form VII was in Hindi or in English. That it was the duty of Food Safety Officer to fill up Form VII. That he did not remember the ingredients which were mentioned in the Form No. VII due to the lapse of time. That as per his report "Added vegetable oil" was found, which was not declared as ingredient because BR of the extracted facts exceeds the prescribed maximum limit of Coconut oil ie 35.5, which clearly shows that some vegetable oil has been added in the sample. I heard the submissions of both the sides and perused the record.
texts.arguments: Rule 37A reads as under: "37-A. Manufacture of proprietary foods and infant foods: (1) An article of infant milk substitutes/ infant foods whose standards are not prescribed in Appendix 'B' shall be manufactured for sale, exhibited for sale or stored for sale only after obtaining the approval of such article of food and its label from Government of India. (2) In case of proprietary foods the name of the food or category under which it falls in these rules shall be mentioned on the label Explanation :- For the purpose of this rule : (a) and (aa) (infant food & infant) ..... Omitted (b) "Proprietary food", means a food which has not been standardised under the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules, 1955." The provisions read as under: "23. Power of the Central Government to make rules.-- (1) The Central Government may, after consultation with the Committee and after previous publication by notification in the Official Gazette, make rules to carry out the provisions of this Act: .......... (1A) In particular and without prejudice to the generality of the foregoing power, such rules may provide for all or any of the following matters, namely:-- .......... (ee) defining the laboratories where samples of articles of food or adulterants may be analysed by public analysts under this Act, .......... Da vs Jagjit Singh on 20 August, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/109557362/ 6 (hh) defining the methods of analysis", 16. Vide notification of the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare dated 25.03.2008, under section Section 23 of the 1954 Act, the Central Government has incorporated Rule 4(9) in the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules, 1955, which read as under: "The manuals of method of analysis brought out by Ministry of Health and Family Welfare shall be adopted for analysing the samples of food articles. In M/s Nestle India Ltd. Vs. The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India & Ors., 2015 2 FAC 56, the above said notification has been held to be ultra vires the PFA Act and the same was not held to be rules having statutory force due to non compliance with section 24(3) of PFA Act. 17. In Pepsico India(supra), the Hon'ble Apex Court considered the issue. The Hon'ble Apex Court while deciding the case, formulated the following questions for consideration: "(1) In the absence of any prescribed and validated method of analysis under Section 23(1-A)(hh) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954, hereinafter referred to as "the 1954 Act", could a prosecution have been launched against the Appellants based on a report submitted by the Public Analyst using the method of the Directorate General of Health Services (D.G.H.S.)? (2) Could a prosecution have been launched against the Appellants in the absence of any validated method of analysis to ascertain the percentage of pesticide residue present in a Carbonated beverage, which renders the report of the Public Analyst unreliable, particularly when it does not indicate that such percentage of the pesticide residue is injurious to health and, therefore, adulterated within the meaning of Section 2(ia) (h) of the aforesaid Act? (3) What is the effect of non-specification of the level of tolerance in respect of the presence of pesticide residue in Sweetened Carbonated Water in the Table appended to Rule 65(2) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules, 1955, hereinafter referred to as "the 1955 Rules"? and (4) What is the liability of the Directors of a company which is said to have committed defaults within the meaning of Section 17 of the 1954 Act, in the light of the decision of this Court in S.M.S. Pharmaceuticals Ltd. Vs. Neeta Bhalla & Anr. [2005 (8) sec 89], when they were neither in charge of nor responsible Da vs Jagjit Singh on 20 August, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/109557362/ 7 for the conduct of the business of the Company?" The relevant observations of Hon'ble Supreme Court are as under: "34. 18. The ratio of Pepsico India (supra) was followed in R. Gopalakrishnan Vs. Food Inspector, Crl. Rev. No. 671/200 dated 17.07.2013 by Hon'ble Kerala High Court and it was observed that the observations made in Pepsico India (supra) were not limited to the subject matter of the appeal Da vs Jagjit Singh on 20 August, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/109557362/ 8 before the Hon'ble Apex Court in the said case but a general preposition of law was laid down. Against the said judgment of Hon'ble Kerala High Court, criminal appeal bearing No. 2476/2014 was preferred, which was also dismissed. Relying upon the judgment of Pepsico India (supra), Hon'ble Kerala High Court in Sanjay Parmanand (supra) held as under: "6. In this case, admittedly, the laboratory for the analysis of food item was not defined and no validated method of analysis of the food item was specified as mandated under Section 23 (1-A) (ee) and (hh) of the P.F.A. Act. (supra). It was held by the Supreme Court in Pepsico India Holdings (supra) that since the Laboratories were not notified and the tests conducted by such laboratories were not admissible in evidence, no prosecution could be based on such report and the accused was entitled to get acquittal. In the decision of this Court in Gopalakrishnan v. Food Inspector [2013 (3) KLT 455], the court relied on the decision of the Supreme Court in Pepsico India Holdings (supra) and found that the Public Analyst's report was not admissible in evidence and accordingly, the Court acquitted the accused. The matter was referred to a Division Bench and the Division Bench also affirmed the said decision, submitted by the learned counsel for the petitioners and the learned Public Prosecutor. Even otherwise, in view of the decision in Pepsico India Holdings (supra), the conviction in this case cannot be sustained as no laboratory was notified and no validated method of analysis was specified as mandated under Section 23 (1-A) (ee) and (hh) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954." 19. Hon'ble Bombay High Court in M/s Nestle India Ltd. Vs. The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India & Ors., 2015 2 FAC 56 , following the judgment of Pepsico India (supra) held that in the absence of designated laboratories and validated methods of analysis, the reports of Public Analyst and Director, CFL cannot be relied upon. Again, Hon'ble Rajasthan High Court in ITC Limited & Anr. Vs. State of Rajasthan Through P.P., 2018 2 FAC 28, held that the provisions of section 23(1A) (ee) & (hh) of PFA were mandatory and in the absence of designated laboratories and specified methods of analysis, the prosecution under section 16 of PFA was bad. Similar view was again taken in Mohanan P. & Ors. Vs. State of Kerala & Anr., 2022 1 FAC 322 by Hon'ble Kerala High Court. Further, in Hindustan Lever Limited Vs. A. Nayak, Food Inspector Rourkela Municipality & Anr., 2021 1 FAC 320, the prosecution launched on the basis of Public Analyst report following DGHS method for violation of section 7(1) read with section 2(ia)(m) of PFA was [LEAKAGE_MASK] for non prescription of methods of analysis under section 23(1A)(hh) of PFA Act. 20 . The observations made by Hon'ble Bombay High Court in Nestle India (supra) read as under: Da vs Jagjit Singh on 20 August, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/109557362/ 9 "93. ..........Upon conjoint reading of both these sections quoted hereinabove, it is clear that under section 3(p), "food laboratory" is a laboratory which is either State or Central laboratory or any other allied laboratory which is accredited and recognized by NABL and by the Food Authority under section 43 of the Act. Sub-section (1) of section 43 makes it abundantly clear that only in that laboratory which is recognized by the Food Authority by Notification, food can be sent for analysis by the Food Analyst. The Apex Court in Pepsico India Holdings Private Limited vs. Food Inspector and Another1 has observed that the provisions are under section mandatory. The Apex Court in this case held that provisions 23(1-A)(ee) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 for testing the food samples/adulteration are mandatory and not directory. This is more so when Section 43(1) is read with the definition of the words "food laboratory" in Section 3(p) of the FSS Act, 2006. The Apex Court in Pepsico India Holding Private Limited (supra) has observed in para 44 as under:- "44. The High Court also misconstrued the provisions of Sections 23(1-A)(ee) and (hh) in holding that the same were basically enabling provisions and were 1 (2011) 1 SCC 176 WPL/1688/2015 not mandatory and could, in any event, be solved by the Central Government by framing the Rules thereunder, by which specified tests to be held in designated laboratories could be spelt out. Consequently, the High Court also erred in holding that the non formulation of rules under the aforesaid provisions of the 1954 Act could not be said to be fatal for the prosecution." The contention of Mr. Khambatta, the learned Senior Counsel appearing on behalf of Respondent Nos. 3 and 4 that only imported food could be tested in the notified laboratories therefore cannot be accepted... Similarly, so far as the food which is manufactured in India is concerned though it is not mentioned that it has to be tested in a notified laboratory, in view of definition of section 3(p) and more particularly the mandate given in section 43(1), the Food Analyst has to analyse the food only in such laboratory which is defined under section 3(p) and recognized by the Food Authority under section 43(1) of the Act."
